title: Don't Make the Thing, the Thing
author: Claire Stoneman
summary: Claire Stoneman warns school and department leaders against a specific CPD failure mode: rolling out a list of high-leverage strategies -- cold call, turn and talk, I Do We Do You Do -- without ever explaining or showing why they work, so that the strategy becomes an empty compliance box rather than a vehicle for thought. She's explicit that codified strategy lists themselves are valuable and have supercharged improvement in her own school; the danger is specifically in how they're rolled out, and she draws on her own early-career mistakes -- mini plenaries, carousel activities, and a 'poetry pass the parcel' she now cringes at -- as examples of doing things mechanically because they were expected, without understanding why. Her diagnostic test for whether a strategy has become an empty 'Thing' is whether it produces a proxy of compliance (a poster on the wall, a stamp in an exercise book, a turn-and-talk performed the moment a leader walks in) rather than genuine teacher and pupil thought. Her prescription for leaders is to model their own thinking explicitly in CPD -- through specific, subject-grounded questions like when to use mini whiteboards, how to anticipate a particular Macbeth misconception, or what to do if a majority of a Year 11 class gets a straight-line-angles question wrong -- rather than delivering a generic, broad-brush strategy list.
points: Stoneman's core distinction -- the strategy itself vs. the strategy becoming an unthinking 'Thing' -- separates a critique of implementation from a critique of the underlying high-leverage-strategy approach, which she explicitly endorses.

Her self-critical examples from her own early career (mini plenaries, carousels, a 'poetry pass the parcel') give the argument credibility by showing she's diagnosing a mistake she made herself, not just criticising other leaders from a distance.

The specific 'proxy' markers she names -- branded wall posters, a 'mini whiteboard activity' stamp, a turn-and-talk performed only when a leader walks in -- give observers concrete, checkable signs that a strategy has become performative rather than genuine.

Her prescription to replace generic strategy CPD with subject-specific worked questions (a particular Macbeth misconception, a specific straight-line-angles error pattern) operationalises 'model your thinking' into something leaders can actually plan and deliver.
quotes: Many schools now have a list of things they do in classrooms. Essentially, strategies they use – perhaps cold call, or turn and talk, or no opt out, or I Do, We Do, You Do.
I’m fine with a list of high leverage strategies that can work right across school. This is important and can supercharge school improvement, and we’ve done this in my own school.
The mini plenary became the Thing. The carousel activity became the Thing. The godawful poetry pass the parcel became the Thing.
It's vitally important that teachers think. School leaders, prioritise your colleagues' thought.
Teachers chucking in a turn and talk when a school leader walks into the room so the school leader can tick it off a list is a proxy, a Thing.
Unless the strategies and tools translate into teacher thought and – crucially – pupil thought (because that's why we're doing what we're doing, right?), we're just fiddling while Rome burns.
Don’t unintentionally make the thing, the Thing. Make thought the thing.
